newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Feb 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Feb 7.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Friday:
* Western Resources Inc is expected to announce within the next few days its acquisition of Kansas City Power and Light for $2 billion in stock, people familiar with the deal say.

* News Analysis: Some hail the merger between Morgan Stanley and Dean Witter as the shape of things to come, but it may be a step back, because Dean Witter is not considered a leader in broker innovations such as electronic trading and new investment products.
* Minutes of the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee meeting show that Fed policy makers were unusually concerned about the high level of stock prices.
* Merchants reported strong sales increases for January, although sales a year earlier were affected by bad weather.
* The German jobless rate soared last month, surprising economists and posing a challenge for Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
* Morgan Stanley shareholders appear to be getting the better deal in the merger with Dean Witter. -- Market Place.
* Jayhawk Acceptance said it would file for bankruptcy after Fleet Financial cut off its access to new money.

* The Securities and Exchange Commission said a real estate investor has been convicted of insider trading and could face a fine of up to $2.85 million for his part in a 1987 incident involving a former Oppenheimer & Co broker.
* Reinhard Richter, a former executive at Archer Daniels Midland, has been indicted on charges that he used false invoices to steal more than $180,000 from the company.
* NEC said it had developed the world's most sophisticated memory chip, a four-gigabit dynamic random access memory chip.

* The Clinton Administration wants to finance its proposals to cut middle class taxes and increase education spending by raising taxes on multinational corporations, ending favorable tax treatment on extra-long-term bonds and raising capital gains taxes.
* John O'Quinn, the lawyer who has played a central role in the lawsuits over silicone breast implants, faces problems over the operation of his tax-exempt private foundation.
* Sotheby's said it had suspended executives in connection with accusations of art smuggling.

* America Online said it would add 50,000 more computer modems to its service that would increase its daily capacity by 60 percent. The company also posts quarterly loss of $154.8 million, or $1.64 a share.
* Reebok's lawsuit against Sony's TriStar Pictures offers a revealing glance about the advertising method known as product placement in Hollywood movies. -- New York newsdesk 212-859-1610
